blocks.text: The chapter defines faith through assurance and conviction, then develops that description through testimony, seeking God, and the actions of many scriptural figures. Its examples include deliverance and achievement, but also torture, imprisonment, death, and promises not yet received. This keeps faith from being reduced to wishful thinking or a guarantee of prosperity. The witness list also includes Sarah, Moses’ parents, Rahab, women who received their dead, and unnamed sufferers; these figures belong within the chapter’s remembered community of witnesses.

Rahab appears alongside the fall of Jericho because she received the spies peacefully. Later Christian connections involving Rahab and “rest” should be kept distinct from Hebrews’ own presentation of land and covenant claims here.

For Hebrews as a whole, Papyrus 46 is an early substantial manuscript witness, though it has missing portions and its date is only approximate. Codex Sinaiticus also preserves Hebrews, placing it after 2 Thessalonians in its New Testament sequence.
